content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes Token Turing Machines (TTMs), a memory-augmented transformer architecture inspired by Neural Turing Machines (NTMs). Experiments on two datasets show the model performs comparably or better than the baselines selected by the authors.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths:**
- The proposed approach is simple and easy to understand
- Memory-augmented neural networks are an under-explored topic and augmenting transformer-based architectures with writeable memory is a promising approach for overcoming some of their limitations.

**Weaknesses**
- The ideas presented here seem to be completely subsumed by past works. For example, the token summarization appears to be identical or closely related to the ISAB block introduced in [1] and adopted in [2].
- There is little to take away or learn from this paper. I have no idea if the model presented here is as generally useful as the authors claim, and it certainly does not seem to be a significant leap in the application domains studied. This is because there is a major disconnect between the paper's stated goals (introducing a general-purpose model that can efficiently handle long input sequences) and experiments (comparisons to other models on two datasets and a limited ablation study using the same data). There are numerous widely used benchmarks to assess the ability of a model to generalize to long sequences, perform algorithmic reasoning, etc. The authors should revisit the work on which their's builds to understand how to better design more informative experiments.
- The related work section is nowhere near sufficient. The authors don't discuss any of the follow-up work on NTMs, even that by the original authors [3].

**References**
1. [Set Transformer: A Framework for Attention-based Permutation-Invariant Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.00825)
2. [Perceiver: General Perception with Iterative Attention](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v139/jaegle21a.html)
3. [Hybrid computing using a neural network with dynamic external memory](https://clgiles.ist.psu.edu/IST597/materials/slides/papers-memory/2016-graves.pdf)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is reasonably easy to understand, but there are various statements that are not correct (the authors seem confused about the difference between sequential and auto-regressive), wholly subjective (that the NTM has been forgotten), or not backed up by evidence (we have not witnessed training instabilities). The novelty of the ideas presented in this work is extremely limited. There are details included about the optimization process in the Appendix, but reproducibility would be greatly improved by releasing code or more thoroughly describing the experimental setup and evaluations.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents known ideas using slightly different terminology/framing, the experiments are disconnected from the stated motivations, and I do not feel as if I learned anything new reading the paper. As such, I recommend rejection.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper introduces Token Turing Machine (TTM), a recurrent neural architecture inspired by, and is a conceptual extension of the Neural Turing Machine: At each step, the model reads a set of input tokens and a set of memory tokens, produces a set of output tokens, and updates the memory tokens. The operations are based on attention and Transformers. This allows linear complexity w.r.t. data sequence length. Experiments on activity detection on video and robot learning confirm the effectiveness of TTM.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
=======
- The proposed TTM is conceptually simple.
- The results seem to support the claims.

Weaknesses
==========
- Some elements of the idea have been known in the literature. There are no surprising elements to be learnt from.
- The experiments can be more comprehensive to confirm the versality of the new design, e.g., on a very long text.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- I would consider the paper to be an extension of LSTM, where the input, output and memory are set of tokens rather than single vectors.
 -The idea of upgrading vectors to matrices (which are set of tokens of fixed length) has been studied before, e.g., [1].
- The idea of data summarization to save computation on memory-augmented neural networks has been suggested and theoretically analyzed in [2].
- Eq (8) on the memory writing doesn't seem to maintain any original order of memory token. Although information doesn't seem to be lost but conceptually this makes it less a "memory" (which in theory should maintain some location-based information).

References:
[1] Do, Kien, Truyen Tran, and Svetha Venkatesh. "Learning deep matrix representations." arXiv preprint arXiv:1703.01454 (2017).
[2] Le, Hung, Truyen Tran, and Svetha Venkatesh. "Learning to remember more with less memorization." ICLR (2020).
content.summary_of_the_review: This is a neat architecture with conceptually simple design and clear semantics. The empirical results support the claims, even though I would like to see something very new to learn from, and a  more comprehensive suite of experiments to confirm the versality of the design, e.g., in long-text processing.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes Token Turing Machines (TTM), a sequential Transformer-based model equipped with an external memory for real-world streaming inference problems. The memory is efficiently read and written at each timestep, together with a Transformer processing unit. The read and write operations are computed based on a token summarisation module, which is much simpler than the operations of NTM and helps TTM obtain bounded computational cost at each timestep.  TTM outperforms competing for online temporal activity localisation methods from videos and robot action policy learning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
- The paper proposes an elegant method to incorporate external memories into the Transformers to deal with streaming inference problems. 
- The proposed method is simple (compared to the Neural Turing Machines) and requires bounded computational cost at each timestep. 
- The experiments are interesting and clearly show the advantages of TTM compared with competing methods. Attempting to work with real robots is encouraging. 
- The paper is generally well-written and easy to follow. 
### Weakness
- There are several confusing details of the method (see questions)
- The baseline set lacks advanced memory-based counterparts

### Comments and questions:
-  About the token summarisation
1. During reading, memory tokens and input tokens are summarised into a small number of tokens before being processed by the Transformers. This token summarisation process is computed based on sets of importance weights. It would be more informative if the authors compared the importance weights of memory tokens and input tokens to show that TTM respects the information stored in the external memory. In short, a more careful ablation study regarding the importance weights is appreciated. 
2. In Section 2.1.4, the authors wrote: “Therefore, the tokens in memory will be erased if they are not re-selected”. As far as I understand from Eq. (1), (2) and (3), token summarisation is not about hard-selecting which tokens to be kept or eliminated; instead, it summarises the tokens by taking weighted sums of them. The authors should rewrite to clarify this point. 
3. The token summarisation plays an essential role in TTM. It would be better if the authors could provide a more detailed analysis of why token summarisation is suitable for the case of TTM. A possible question to be concerned with is why we can use only 16-32 tokens for summarising more than 3000 tokens at each timestep. 
-  About the experiments
1. Results related to TTM should be highlighted for ease of reading. 
2. It is well-known that memory-augmented neural networks, e.g., the Neural Turing Machines, may drastically increase training time. It would be appreciated if the authors could provide a comparison of the training time of TTM and other competing methods. 
3. Can the authors explain why TTM is worse than memoryless TTM in the Knock task in the robot learning experiment?
4. Baseline: The idea of augmenting Transformer with external memory is not new. Please compare with other memory-augmented Transformers [1,2] to show the benefit of the proposed approach.
5. Ablation study: NTM is not a strong baseline for read/write operation. It is better to compare with improved read/write methods, such as [3]

[1] Rae, Jack W., Anna Potapenko, Siddhant M. Jayakumar, Chloe Hillier, and Timothy P. Lillicrap. "Compressive Transformers for Long-Range Sequence Modelling." In International Conference on Learning Representations. 2019.

[2] Burtsev, Mikhail S., Yuri Kuratov, Anton Peganov, and Grigory V. Sapunov. "Memory Transformer." arXiv e-prints (2020): arXiv-2006.

[3] Le, Hung, Truyen Tran, and Svetha Venkatesh. "Learning to Remember More with Less Memorization." In International Conference on Learning Representations. 2018.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is overall clear, with some details needing more description. The architecture as a whole is reasonably novel, although the general idea and model parts are reused from prior works. It may be non-trivial to implement the method and reproduce the result (no code and algorithm provided).
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents a fascinating modernisation of the Neural Turing Machine. Well-motivated modifications and choice of components lead to better results in real-world streaming inference problems. However, there are limitations in the experiment's baselines and clarity in the method to make work reproducible.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents the Token Turing Machine (TTM), which is a standard transformer augmented with an external memory matrix inspired by the Neural Turing Machine (NTM). Like NTM, TTM reads and writes a memory matrix through differentiable operations on each step. TTM uses attention-based summarization operations to perform the reads and writes, and (unlike NTM) uses a transformer instead of an RNN as the controller. TTM is evaluated against baseline models on two tasks:  Charades (video activity localization) and SayCan (robotic manipulation). The experimental results show improvement over baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

Motivated by the significant potential utility of external memory, especially for transformers which (unlike RNNs) lack recurrent memory, TTM represents an updated attempt at realizing the goals of NTM and its ambitious successor the Differentiable Neural Computer (DNC), while extending transformers in a useful way. The key contribution of TTM is a particular way of performing memory reads and writes through matrix-to-matrix operations that can be viewed as summarization or compression of data. The two tasks chosen for evaluation (Charades and SayCan) are challenging, cutting-edge applications of transformers, so the results are of current interest.


**Weaknesses**

The details of the TTM model are inadequately explained. The first problem is the choice of terminology. The NTM paper explained their model in standard terms of vectors and matrices, but this paper chooses instead to call vectors “tokens”, and matrices “sets of tokens”. This makes “token summarization” sound exotic, when it’s actually just a matrix-to-matrix operation based on attention. The terminology is important, because the memory read and write functions of both NTM and DNC are also matrix-to-matrix operations based on attention, and this fact needs to be addressed directly rather than obscured.

Section 2.1.1, describing the summarization function, is very unclear. Does each instance of the index $i$ in the equations iterate over the $p$ incoming vectors, or does $i$ sometimes iterate over the $k$ outgoing vectors? What dimension is the softmax performed over? How is $k$ chosen? Is it a hyperparameter? Are the $k$ tokens selected as the highest weighted? What does it mean to learn a matrix $Q$ to obtain a matrix $W$? Because the summarization function is the core technical contribution of the work, this section needs to be crystal clear.

What is meant by the many references to the “backbone”, and how is this backbone related to the TTM architecture?

A search for “transformer memory” returns many papers attempting to add external memory to transformers. One example of a transformer with an external memory matrix, applied to RL tasks, is the Working Memory Graph. See also Recurrent Independent Mechanisms. TTM needs to be carefully distinguished from these prior works.

The experiments in the NTM and DNC papers were carefully justified for the special demands they place on memory, but this paper does not make similar arguments justifying its selection of the Charades and SayCan tasks. There also need to be some targetted diagnostic tasks (as in the NTM and DNC papers) to demonstrate that TTM’s memory matrix does indeed function as designed. 

The Charades and SayCan tasks don’t provide good evidence of TTM’s usefulness. The best Charades model in Table 1 was I3D + CTRN, not TTM. The discussion drew a distinction between offline and online models, but did not explain why online models are important for Charades. In Table 2, several baseline transformers perform nearly as well as TTM, such as the Causal Transformer with 96 tokens, which also costs far fewer operations than TTM with $n=3136$. For the SayCan tasks this work adds “controls for base motion”, which would seem to require re-training and re-tuning of the baseline models to enable fair comparisons. But hyperparameter tuning is not discussed at all.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity**

As noted above, important information is missing. In addition, the paper contains many awkward and confusing phrases:

“we do not want to run our entire transformer model for each time step when a new observation is provided”

“in contrast to most previous recurrent models (e.g., RNNs) directly digesting history vectors”

“long-range videos”

“We focus on making online inferences”

“the memory of our model are actually the historical observations of the model”



**Quality**

The overall quality of the paper is low, for reasons explained above.

**Novelty**

As explained above, many external memory architectures (including some based on transformers) have performed memory reads and writes by means of some form of attention. As another such model, TTM’s novelty is unclear.

**Reproducibility**

I find no indication that source code will be provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: The motivation and general direction of TTM are interesting, as evidenced by the large number of similar prior attempts. But this work appears to be at a very early and rough stage. Addressing its weaknesses will require time and effort, but I look forward to seeing the results.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

display_title: This is a computer vision / robotics paper.

content.title: This is a computer vision / robotics paper.
content.comment:
We would like to clarify that this is a computer vision / robotics paper, and that our objective is to make the memory model understand real-world visual data.

One of the most important contributions of the paper in fact is that we made our Turing machine learn from a real-world video input, training it for activity detection as well as robot learning tasks. This is in contrast to the previous works cited/mentioned, which limited themselves to text analysis or simple image processing like MNIST.

We are withdrawing this paper to give it an opportunity to be reviewed at a conference that better understands the paper (and Transformer models).

We will provide more detailed rebuttals to the reviewer comments in the following week.
